One method we are currently considering is to build single series models for each variable, using the methods of Box and Jenkins (1970) for example, and then searching for relationships between series by relating the residuals from these single models.

sections.summary: The paper opens by contrasting frequently reported time-series regressions with high R2 and low Durbin-Watson statistics against textbook warnings about autocorrelated errors. It lists three consequences of autocorrelated errors and announces that the paper will focus on invalid significance tests and the possibility of spurious relationships.

sections.summary: The authors review stationary ARMA and ARIMA models, introduce white noise and differencing, and argue that many economic series are highly autocorrelated or near random walks, so d is very often one. This time-series foundation motivates why standard regression assumptions about errors and regressors are likely to fail.
sections.title: Time-Series Representation of Economic Variables

sections.summary: The paper sets up the usual linear regression model and the F-test for no relationship. If Y and X are nonstationary or highly autocorrelated, the residuals inherit that autocorrelation, so F does not follow Fisher's F distribution under the null. The independent AR(1) case and Kendall's variance result are used to show that high R2 can occur by chance.

sections.summary: A simulation study regresses independent random walks and other series. The first experiment shows that a t-test rejects no relationship far too often, and the standard error of the coefficient is heavily underestimated. A second experiment varies the number of independent regressors and shows rejection rates rising sharply for random walks and A.R.I.M.A. (0,1,1) levels, with high R2 and low d.
sections.title: Simulation Evidence for Spurious Regressions

source_span.end_text: This provides an indication of just how one can be misled by regressions

sections.summary: The discussion concludes that strongly autocorrelated residuals imply a mis-specified equation, whatever R2 is. It reviews possible remedies, recommends first differences for highly autocorrelated variables, and suggests building models with both levels and changes. Sheppard's U.K. consumption regressions illustrate how differencing can overturn conclusions.
sections.title: Discussion: Mis-specification, Differencing, and Reinterpretation

sections.summary: The authors distinguish a time-series analyst's good theory, which requires white-noise residuals, from econometric theories that may be unspecific about lag structure and residual properties. They argue that levels-only high-R2 regressions make testing further variables impossible, while changes often lower R2 and permit more experimentation.
sections.title: Theory, Structural Models, and the Case for Changes
